top_stories.title: Tether lands first full KPMG audit, ending an 8-year wait
points: KPMG US issued an unqualified "clean" opinion on Tether International's complete 2025 financial statements — the first full audit (a comprehensive, standards-based examination of financial statements, stricter than a limited attestation) since Tether promised one in 2017.

The audit validated $6.8 billion in excess reserves over liabilities at year-end 2025, on a reserve base reported above $120 billion backing USDT (Tether's stablecoin — a crypto token designed to hold a fixed $1 value).
Auditors physically counted every gold bar in reserves rather than relying on custodian reports; coverage spans cash, securities and other collateral.
Tether previously published only periodic attestations (limited third-party spot checks) from BDO Italia, fueling more than a decade of fractional-reserve suspicion since its 2015 launch.
The result answers regulatory demands that stablecoins prove adequate backing before use in regulated financial systems, and pressures rivals like USDC to match the standard.

unique_angles.point: Tether paid $18.5M to the New York AG and $41M to the CFTC in 2021 to settle earlier claims about its reserve disclosures.
USDT handles roughly 85% of global stablecoin trading volume, so a run on inadequate reserves could have cascaded across thousands of exchanges — a risk the audit now defuses.

items.title: Baltimore sues Kalshi and Polymarket over unlicensed gambling
points: The city filed consumer-protection suits alleging both prediction markets (platforms where users trade contracts on real-world event outcomes) run unlicensed sports gambling via event contracts.
The Kalshi suit also names Coinbase, Robinhood and Webull for distributing Kalshi contracts inside their apps.
Polymarket was sued separately over an internal market-making team allegedly trading against its own users.
Baltimore seeks penalties, restitution and injunctions; Kalshi says it is a regulated, transparent marketplace and will defend the claims.

items.title: EigenLabs launches Yukon Research, an AI-human competition platform
points: Distributed teams of humans and AI agents compete on verifiable science benchmarks scored by deterministic sandbox evaluations (automated tests that always produce the same result) and merged into shared repositories.
In the ECDSA.fail challenge, participants beat Google Quantum AI's benchmark by 50.3% within 8 hours.
Other results: a 9.5x throughput gain for Lighter exchange's prover and a 3.5x post-quantum Ethereum scaling improvement.

Partners include Stanford, UC Berkeley, Princeton, the Ethereum Foundation and Lighter Exchange; open challenges cover ZK proof acceleration (speeding up cryptographic proofs that verify computations without revealing data), Apple-silicon inference and open CS problems.

items.title: Coinbase ships new Deribit matching engine
points: The rebuilt engine processes 100,000+ orders per second with sub-millisecond latency (under one thousandth of a second between order submission and execution).

items.title: Memecoin market shrinks even as launchpads grow
points: Pump.fun's launchpad market share fell from 79.4% in late June to 26.7% in mid-July amid Robinhood Chain competition, then recovered to 51.7% by early August.
Its fee revenue rose 30% ($24.45M to $31.83M) but the launchpad category grew 77%, so Pump.fun lost relative ground; Pons on Robinhood Chain took second place with $19.80M in 30 days.
The memecoin sector sits at $25.15B, down 83% from a December 2024 peak of $150.6B.
Only 34% of 5,774 tracked tokens gained value over 30 days, and the median token is down 99% from its all-time high despite a volume surge.

items.title: Jim Cramer sells Bitcoin over quantum computing fears
points: Cramer exited BTC citing quantum risk (future quantum computers potentially breaking Bitcoin's cryptography), though IBM's timeline puts that 3-4 years out.
Bitcoin rose 1.6% on the news.

issues.subject: Tether Just Got Its First Full Audit From KPMG

headlines: Tether completed its first full audit by KPMG, a major accounting firm, addressing years of skepticism about whether the stablecoin (a cryptocurrency designed to maintain a fixed value) actually holds sufficient reserves to back its issued tokens.
The audit provides institutional confidence in Tether's $120+ billion reserve backing, critical for the broader crypto market since Tether is the most-used stablecoin for trading and liquidity.
KPMG's findings validate Tether's claims about asset reserves, potentially ending debates about fractional reserve practices that have plagued the company since its 2015 launch.

sections.title: Tether's Audit Milestone
points: 1. KPMG, a Big Four accounting firm, conducted the first full comprehensive audit of Tether's reserves, confirming backing for its USDT stablecoin in circulation.
2. Tether has previously used attestations (limited third-party verification) rather than full audits, leaving questions about whether reserves truly matched issued tokens.
3. The full audit covers all asset classes held as collateral, including cash, securities, and other holdings, providing transparency investors have demanded for over a decade.
4. This audit addresses regulatory pressure from governments and institutions requiring proof that stablecoins maintain adequate backing before they can be used in regulated financial systems.

sections.title: Market Implications
points: 1. Tether's USDT handles approximately 85% of all stablecoin trading volume globally, making reserve verification essential for crypto market stability.
2. The audit removes a major technical risk: if reserves were inadequate, a run on Tether could trigger cascading losses across thousands of trading platforms and exchanges.
3. Institutional investors and regulated custodians can now use Tether with higher confidence, potentially accelerating crypto adoption in traditional finance.
4. Competitors like USDC and other stablecoins face pressure to undergo similar audits or lose institutional credibility.
